claim: SARS-CoV-2 was classified as a global pandemic by the WHO on March 11, 2020.
source: On March 11, 2020, the World Health Organization (WHO) classified the SARS-CoV-2 virus (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2) as a global pandemic due to its rapid spread and high infection rate (Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2020

claim: Nearly 15.8 million SARS-CoV-2 sequences have been deposited into the GISAID database as of July 21, 2023.
source: Consequently, nearly 15.8 million SARS-CoV-2 sequences have been deposited into the 'Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data' database (as of July 21, 2023, GISAID).
evidence: Supported by reference to GISAID database as of a specific date

claim: The 'Coronavirus-Surveillanceverordnung' (CorSurV) was enacted by the State Ministry of Health on January 19, 2021.
source: In Germany, the 'Coronavirus-Surveillanceverordnung' (CorSurV) enacted by the State Ministry of Health on January 19, 2021, mandated that laboratories with sequencing capabilities process SARS-CoV-2-positive samples, offering financial compensation until April 2023 (Corona-Surveillanceverordnung, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Corona-Surveillanceverordnung, 2022

claim: PANGO provides a standard naming convention for SARS-CoV-2 lineages based on unique mutation profiles.
source: For keeping track of the rapid SARS-CoV-2 evolution, PANGO (Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak) provides a standard naming convention based on unique mutation profiles and further criteria, resulting in the classification of over 3660 lineages (as of August 2023) (Rambaut et al., 2020; PANGO, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rambaut et al., 2020 and PANGO, 2023

claim: Over 3660 SARS-CoV-2 lineages have been classified as of August 2023.
source: For keeping track of the rapid SARS-CoV-2 evolution, PANGO (Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak) provides a standard naming convention based on unique mutation profiles and further criteria, resulting in the classification of over 3660 lineages (as of August 2023) (Rambaut et al., 2020; PANGO, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rambaut et al., 2020 and PANGO, 2023

claim: The Alpha lineage (B.1.1.7) was the first defined VOC.
source: The first defined VOC (now de-escalated), the Alpha lineage, rapidly replaced almost all previously circulating lineages globally by the end of 2020 until the VOC Delta (main lineage B.1.617.2) replaced it in mid-2021 (Washington et al., 2021; Walker et al., 2021; Michaelsen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Washington et al., 2021; Walker et al., 2021; Michaelsen et al., 2022

claim: The Alpha lineage rapidly replaced almost all previously circulating lineages globally by the end of 2020.
source: The first defined VOC (now de-escalated), the Alpha lineage, rapidly replaced almost all previously circulating lineages globally by the end of 2020 until the VOC Delta (main lineage B.1.617.2) replaced it in mid-2021 (Washington et al., 2021; Walker et al., 2021; Michaelsen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Washington et al., 2021; Walker et al., 2021; Michaelsen et al., 2022

claim: The VOC Delta (main lineage B.1.617.2) replaced the Alpha lineage in mid-2021.
source: The first defined VOC (now de-escalated), the Alpha lineage, rapidly replaced almost all previously circulating lineages globally by the end of 2020 until the VOC Delta (main lineage B.1.617.2) replaced it in mid-2021 (Washington et al., 2021; Walker et al., 2021; Michaelsen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Washington et al., 2021; Walker et al., 2021; Michaelsen et al., 2022

claim: Thuringia is a rural federal state in central Germany with a population of 2.1 million and no major airports.
source: Thuringia is a rural federal state in central Germany with a population of 2.1 million and no major airports (overview of Thuringia's population density in Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing population density

claim: The study used 289,487 public SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Germany (excluding Thuringia) including 137,024 Alpha genomes.
source: To understand its spread, we used 289,487 public SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Germany (excluding Thuringia; including 137,024 Alpha genomes) and 7394 genomes from our own sequencing data for Thuringia (including 6307 Alpha genomes) to track Alpha's occurrence from December 2020 to August 2021 (see Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Figure 1—source data 1; Figure 1—source data 2; for details, see Methods section 'Alpha spread datasets').
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1 and supplementary materials

claim: The study used 7394 genomes from Thuringia including 6307 Alpha genomes.
source: To understand its spread, we used 289,487 public SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Germany (excluding Thuringia; including 137,024 Alpha genomes) and 7394 genomes from our own sequencing data for Thuringia (including 6307 Alpha genomes) to track Alpha's occurrence from December 2020 to August 2021 (see Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Figure 1—source data 1; Figure 1—source data 2; for details, see Methods section 'Alpha spread datasets').
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1 and supplementary materials

claim: In late December 2020, six federal states in Germany reported the first cases of the Alpha variant.
source: In late December 2020, six federal states in Germany (from here on called states) reported the first cases of the Alpha variant.
evidence: Supported by the study's analysis of genomic data

claim: The Corona-Surveillance regulation was passed at the end of January 2021, leading to a rapid increase in sampling and sequencing by February.
source: However, the Corona-Surveillance regulation was passed at the end of January 2021, leading to a rapid increase in sampling and sequencing by February since sequencing costs could be reimbursed.
evidence: Supported by reference to the regulation and observed increase in sequencing

claim: By March, Alpha had spread to nearly all states and districts in Germany with a median of 76.47% Alpha samples among a federal state's total sequenced samples.
source: By March, Alpha had spread to nearly all states and districts (districts are similar to counties or provinces) in Germany (median: 76.47% Alpha samples among a federal states total sequenced samples compared to 36.03% in February, excluding Thuringia) and Thuringia (median: 85.29 %, up from 50.00% in February).
evidence: Supported by analysis of genomic data

claim: By March, Alpha had spread to Thuringia with a median of 85.29% Alpha samples.
source: By March, Alpha had spread to nearly all states and districts (districts are similar to counties or provinces) in Germany (median: 76.47% Alpha samples among a federal states total sequenced samples compared to 36.03% in February, excluding Thuringia) and Thuringia (median: 85.29 %, up from 50.00% in February).
evidence: Supported by analysis of genomic data

claim: Sequencing declined in Germany including Thuringia during June and July 2021 due to the decrease in overall daily cases.
source: During the summer of June and July 2021, sequencing declined in Germany (including Thuringia; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) due to the decrease in overall daily cases, as reported by Meintrup et al., 2022; Oh et al., 2022.
evidence: Supported by citations to Meintrup et al., 2022; Oh et al., 2022 and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The spread of the Alpha lineage in Thuringia lagged roughly 2 weeks behind the general spread of other German federal states.
source: In summary, the spread of the Alpha lineage in Thuringia lagged roughly 2 weeks behind the general spread of other German federal states but showed similar proportions.
evidence: Supported by analysis of temporal genomic data

claim: Thuringia was among the first states to adopt new containment measures, including contact limitations, closure of retail shops, and prohibition of tourist journeys on December 14, 2020.
source: Thuringia was among the first states to adopt new containment measures, including contact limitations, closure of retail shops, and prohibition of tourist journeys (December 14, 2020).
evidence: Supported by reference to public health measures

claim: Jena was the first German city to implement mandatory public masking in March 2020.
source: Jena, a city in Thuringia, was also the first German city to implement mandatory public masking in March 2020 (Pletz et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pletz et al., 2023

claim: Contacts were further restricted on January 9th, and people were urged to restrict their movement radius to 15 km.
source: Contacts were further restricted on January 9th, and people were urged to restrict their movement radius to 15 km, which might explain the delay besides the absence of major airports nearby.
evidence: Supported by reference to public health measures and inference about delay

claim: All Thuringian genomes were evenly distributed between other German samples in the phylogenetic time tree.
source: All Thuringian genomes were evenly distributed between other German samples in the phylogenetic time tree (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Nine Alpha subclusters were identified out of 70,429 Alpha genomes based on mutation profile, time period, and phylogenetic distance.
source: We identified nine clusters out of 70,429 Alpha genomes, based on their mutation profile, time period, and phylogenetic distance (from here on called Alpha subclusters; for details, see Methods 'Subcluster identification').
evidence: Supported by genomic analysis described in Methods

claim: S:H49Y eases cell entry in S-pseudotyped lentiviral system.
source: S:H49Y eases cell entry in S-pseudotyped lentiviral system (Ozono et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ozono et al., 2021

claim: S:N354K slightly impaired mAb h11B11.
source: S:N354K slightly impaired mAb h11B11 (Du et al., 2021)

evidence: Supported by citations to Liang et al., 2022; Kimura et al., 2022; Asif et al., 2022

claim: S:S939F modulates T-cell propensity.
source: S:S939F: modulates T-cell propensity (Donzelli et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Donzelli et al., 2022

source: Subclusters 6.1 and 7.1 subsequently emerged from the same districts as their parent clusters (6 and 7) after 12 and 13 days, respectively.

claim: The subclusters mainly spread regionally confined and not across all of Thuringia.
source: The subclusters mainly spread regionally confined and not across all of Thuringia (see Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) but were also identified in other states of Germany (see 'https://microreact.org/'-project).

claim: The subclusters were also identified in other states of Germany.
source: The subclusters mainly spread regionally confined and not across all of Thuringia (see Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) but were also identified in other states of Germany (see 'https://microreact.org/'-project).

claim: The 'S:S939F' subcluster spread across 15 states, with the first samples being isolated outside of Thuringia.
source: For example, the 'S:S939F' subcluster spread across 15 states, with the first samples being isolated outside of Thuringia.

claim: The eight Spike-mutation subclusters had expanded between 4 and 12 of the 23 Thuringian districts within the observable time period of each subcluster.
source: The eight Spike-mutation subclusters had expanded between 4 and 12 of the 23 Thuringian districts within the observable time period of each subcluster.
evidence: Supported by geographical analysis of genomic data

claim: The eight Spike-mutation subclusters expanded by one to six districts per month.
source: They expanded by one to six districts per month, with a greater expansion accompanied mainly by a larger increase in the subcluster sample number.

claim: The ORF1b-variant comprised 21 districts and expanded between 2 and 7 districts per month.
source: In contrast, the ORF1b-variant even comprised 21 districts and expanded between 2 and 7 districts per month (see Figure 2a).

claim: Around 200 million trips were used to determine the number of daily trips between the Thuringian districts.
source: Around 200 million trips were used to determine the number of daily trips between the Thuringian districts.

claim: The mobile service data-based assumption of a subcluster's spread aligned well with the subsequent regional coverage of fast-spreading, highly prevalent subclusters, such as subcluster 7.

claim: The assumed spread for the low-prevalence subclusters did not correspond well with the actual occurrence.

claim: BQ.1.1 was first isolated in a northwestern Thuringian community with around 20,000 inhabitants on October 5, 2022.
source: First isolated in a northwestern Thuringian community with around 20,000 inhabitants on October 5, 2022, we identified this particular sublineage on October 14, 2022, among a routine batch of 42 samples.

claim: BQ.1.1 was identified on October 14, 2022, among a routine batch of 42 samples.
source: First isolated in a northwestern Thuringian community with around 20,000 inhabitants on October 5, 2022, we identified this particular sublineage on October 14, 2022, among a routine batch of 42 samples.

claim: 18 communities with high (>10,000), 34 with medium (2001–10,000), and 82 with low (30–2000) number of incoming one-way trips from the originating community were identified.
source: Considering the highest incoming mobility from both datasets, we identified 18 communities with high (>10,000), 34 with medium (2001–10,000), and 82 with low (30–2000) number of incoming one-way trips from the originating community (purple triangles in Figure 3a).

claim: 19 additional samples were collected (isolated between October 17 and October 25, 2022) as part of guided sampling.
source: Subsequently, we collected 19 additional samples (isolated between October 17 and October 25, 2022; see 'Guided Sampling' for October 2022, Figure 3a) besides the randomized sampling strategy.

claim: 132 samples were collected for October (covering dates between the 5th and 31st) as part of general Thuringian surveillance.

claim: 69 samples were collected in November (covering dates between the 1st and 25th) as part of general Thuringian surveillance.
source: As part of the general Thuringian surveillance, we collected 132 samples for October (covering dates between the 5th and 31st) and 69 samples in November (covering dates between the 1st and 25th; see Figure 3b and c).

claim: Among the 19 samples specifically collected based on mobile service data, one additional sample of the Omicron sublineage BQ.1.1 was identified in a community with high incoming mobility.
source: Among the 19 samples specifically collected based on mobile service data, we identified one additional sample of the specific Omicron sublineage BQ.1.1 in a community with high incoming mobility (n=14, number of trips = 37,499) with a distance of approximately 16 km between both towns.

claim: The randomly sampled routine surveillance strategy did not detect another BQ.1.1 sample during October 2022.
source: Our randomly sampled routine surveillance strategy did not detect another sample during the same period.

claim: Only in the 1-month follow-up (November 2022) were four other BQ.1.1 samples identified across Thuringia through routine surveillance.
source: Only in the 1-month follow-up were four other samples identified across Thuringia through routine surveillance (November 2022, Figure 3c).

claim: BQ.1.1's prevalence in Thuringia remained rare with only 42 samples found until June 2023, 8 months after the first occurrence.
source: In our case, BQ.1.1's prevalence in Thuringia was even lower than expected, and it also remained rare in subsequent months, with only 42 samples found until June 2023, 8 months after the first occurrence in Thuringia.

claim: The lack of major transport hubs is a plausible explanation for the delayed spread of the Alpha lineage in Thuringia.
source: A plausible explanation for the delayed spread of the Alpha lineage in Thuringia is the lack of major transport hubs, as Alpha first occurred in federal states with such hubs.

claim: Previous studies have highlighted the impact of major transportation hubs in the spread of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Previous studies have already highlighted the impact of major transportation hubs in the spread of Sars-CoV-2 (Alpert et al., 2021; Tegally et al., 2023).

claim: Mobile service data can support surveillance by retrospectively examining surveillance sampling coverage and possible sampling bias.
source: Mobile service data can support such surveillance in different ways. Previous studies examined the capabilities of mobility data in the context of, e.g., case trajectories, but retrospectively applied to already collected data, it can be used to examine surveillance sampling coverage and possible sampling bias.
evidence: Supported by the study's analysis of mobility data and genomic surveillance

claim: Mobile service data indicated a putative sampling bias and partially predicted the spread of Thuringian subclusters.
source: We exemplified this approach with the Alpha lineage, where mobile service data indicated a putative sampling bias and partially predicted the spread of our Thuringian subclusters.

claim: Actively guiding the sampling process through mobile service data was demonstrated with the proof of principle focusing on the Omicron-lineage BQ.1.1.
source: Another approach is actively guiding the sampling process through mobile service data, which we demonstrated with our proof of principle focusing on the Omicron-lineage BQ.1.1 as a real-life example.
evidence: Supported by the BQ.1.1 guided sampling experiment

claim: The institute sequenced 3770 SARS-CoV-2 samples until June 2023.

claim: SYNLAB Holding Deutschland GmbH, Bioscientia Healthcare GmbH, and DIANOVIS GmbH provided additional 7800 Thuringian SARS-CoV-2 genomes and their metadata.
